steps.label: The fourth electron
lines: In graphite each carbon atom is sp²

steps.why: The whole answer rests on a count. Carbon has four valence electrons and graphite uses only three of them for bonding, so exactly one electron per carbon atom is available for something else.
common_mistakes: Writing that each carbon makes four sigma bonds in graphite. It makes three, and that is what leaves the fourth electron over.
Answering sp³ for graphite. Three bonded neighbours means sp².
steps.memory_tip: Three bonds used, one electron left over, on every carbon atom.
steps.margin_note: Count the bonds first: three sigma bonds out of four valence electrons.

Conduction is much better along a sheet

steps.why: A substance conducts when it holds charged particles that can move. In graphite those particles are the delocalised electrons, and because they are spread along the sheets the current passes far more easily along a layer than across the stack.
common_mistakes: Saying graphite conducts because it contains free ions. Graphite is covalent; the moving charges are electrons, not ions.
Writing that graphite conducts equally in every direction. Conduction along a sheet is much better than conduction across the sheets.
steps.memory_tip: A delocalised electron is a moving electron, and a moving electron is a current.
steps.margin_note: Name the electron as delocalised and say plainly that it carries the current.

insider_note: A complete answer counts the bonds first — three sigma bonds from four valence electrons — and then says the fourth electron is delocalised over the sheet and carries the current.
